reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In the manuscript entitled “Observation of wave amplification and temporal topological state in a genuine photonic time crystal”, Xiong et al. present an impressive and experimentally rich demonstration of a genuine photonic time crystal (PTC), realized via a dynamically modulated transmission line platform. Through temporal periodic modulation, they succeed in observing the emergence of k-gaps and associated phenomena such as wave amplification. Even more compelling is their direct observation of a temporally localized topological edge state at a domain wall between two distinct PTC phases. The work is well-structured and highly original. I am enthusiastic about its potential impact and would recommend publication, pending the authors' response to the following points:
- Temporally localized topological edge states have previously been demonstrated in a synthetic space (e.g., Ref. 20). The authors should explicitly discuss this earlier work and highlight how their approach differs. That said, to the best of my knowledge, this work indeed represents the first realization of temporally localized topological edge states in a genuine photonic time crystal, as opposed to previous implementations based on synthetic dimensions.
- Line 155, the authors mention that “k gaps open in momentum space”. However, in the measured spectrum in Fig 3b, there is no clear “gap” at k = 0.5, but a dark spot occupying the expected k-gap region. Could the authors elaborate on this? Is it an experimental artifact, or does it point to a more nuanced understanding of how k-gaps manifest in this system?
- Line 195, as the authors mentioned, the system exhibits intrinsic loss. Given that the Floquet band structure is calculated under lossless conditions, how robust is the comparison between theory and experiment? Could the inclusion of loss qualitatively or quantitatively alter the Floquet features?
- The observation of a temporal topological edge state is one of the most exciting aspects of this work. To better understand and reproduce this result, the authors should provide the precise temporal modulation profiles corresponding to the two PTCs with Zak phases of 0 and π, respectively. Also, please include the exact modulation used to form the temporal domain wall.
- In Fig. 1f, the temporal edge state is expected to exhibit nearly unity transmission. Yet in Fig. 4b, the measured |T + R| is close to zero. This striking difference deserves clarification—could it arise from interference effects, mode mismatch, or other loss mechanisms?
- The asymmetry in the temporal edge state profile is intriguing. The authors suggest it stems from intrinsic losses in the transmission line (lines 258–260). Can this be backed up with simulations or theoretical modeling? If so, showing such analysis would greatly strengthen the manuscript.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This is a very timely and interesting study of a time crystalline system experimentally realized in the microwave regime via a transmission line comprising an inductor and a varactor diode element, the latter having bias-controlled capacitance. With a time-modulated bias it hence corresponds to a time-modulated permittivity system.
The authors show a power gain in the system occurring within the k-gap of the time-modulated system, as well as new type of topological edge modes in the phase-space of the time-crystalline system which were observed when an interface is created between the two time crystals, each having a different modulation phase.
This work reports exciting new Physics that I believe will inspire further progress in the field of space-time photonics. I am therefore recommending its publication provided the authors explain more in depth the underlying Physics, while giving more expanded supportive context for the benefit of the reader.
In particular:
(1) The authors state that when the incident wave, this being a broad pulse, hits the transmission line there is power gain around the k-gap coming from the modulation mechanism. They also mention that k-gap in time crystals is analogous to omega-gap in photonic crystals. When incident light within the omega-gap spectrum hits the photonic crystal interface it completely back-reflects. Here when light hits the transmission line it couples in and its intensity enhances in the k-gap spectrum. So, it appears the analogy does not quite work- something is different in their system because the EM can couples into the k-gap modes. Can the authors say a few words what allows the wave to couple into the k-gap modes, instead of getting back-reflected as one would expect from a k-gap behavior.
(2) I think it would be helpful if the authors added a section in the supplemental material explaining the boundary conditions they are considering. In section IV they are talking about temporal boundaries but the modulation is continuous with no discontinuity so I am a bit confused where the temporal boundary (i.e. a discontinuity in permittivity in time) comes from. Also, while the wave goes through the transmission line there are clearly spatial boundaries. Elaborating further these aspects would be very helpful not only in understanding the method but also the results.
(3) Adding to (2): I realize the transmission line has a quasi-static homogenized response, but even if I were to ignore the in between spatial boundaries there are at least two spatial boundaries at the entry and exit of the wave.
(4) How is t0=0 defined? Is it when modulation is switched on?
(5) In Fig. 4 is k_inc=k_0=omega_0/c with omega_0 being the central frequency of the input pulsed signal? Please elaborate.
(6) How is wave vector k inside the time crystal defined/determined? In spatial photonic crystals the frequency is fixed by the input wave and the Floquet-Bloch wave inside the photonic crystal is a sum of various spatial harmonics, i.e., wave vector components, that relate to the spatial modulation (i.e. spatial period a). Here, the Floquet wave inside the time crystal should be a sum of different time harmonics that relate to the modulation frequency, right? In photonic crystals omega is conserved, in time crystals by analogy one would expect k to be conserved. However, Fig. 3(e) could suggest otherwise? The authors should add in the supplemental material a section describing how the wave vector inside the homogenized time-crystal is determined from the input wave.
(7) Related to (6): is the wave vector related to the individual frequency components of the input pulse conserved but only the components around kgap end-up getting amplified at the cost of the other frequency components? I think in the caption of Fig. 3e it should be clarified that "The momenta of the input signal ..." is "The momentum at the central frequency of the input pulsed signal ...”.
(8) Where is the small gain in k_inc observed in Fig. 3(f) coming from?
(9) Related to comment (1): I would expect at a k-gap to see high back-reflection instead of enhancement. In the band structure of the DTL seen in Fig. 3(b) in the region that the authors have terms as k-gaps, one can clearly observe flat segments in the omega versus k dispersion relation, implying domega/dk=0, i.e. frozen-light modes. Slow-light (low-group velocity) modes have been associated with amplification, by observation of enhancement of associated non-linear effects [e.g. see B. Corcoran et al, Nature Photonics volume 3, pages 206–210 (2009)], and other similar effects. Electric field intensity amplification has also been observed directly with simulations in slow-light systems; e.g. see Foteinopoulou+Vigneron, Phys. Rev. B 88, 195144 (2013)]. Could the observed power gain be due to the frozen-light mode in the region the authors term as k-gap (flat omega-k dispersion line) rather than a k-gap effect?
(10) The authors use a model to calculate the permittivity versus the DC bias for different values of DC bias, V, of the varactor. Then they apply this model to find the modulated permittivity epsilon(t) by using each separate value V(t); i.e. the authors have implicitly assumed zero latency in the varactor response. I think it would be useful if the authors added a few words describing why the varactor latency can be considered negligible.
(11) Eq. S.6 has a typo. In the bottom equation second term I think it should be omega_m instead of omega_a.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In the paper, authors experimentally demonstrate both nonhermitian bandgap and temporal topological state at the temporal boundary of two bandgaps with different topologies. Although the former has been demonstrated the latter is a first-time demonstration to my knowledge. They employ a transmission line based method to mimic photonic time crystal in microwave regime. The paper is well structured and written with sufficient technical details provided in the main text and supplementary. Although similar experimental setups have been used in previous proof-of-concept demonstrations of temporally varying media, and the theoretical foundations of topology in photonic time crystals are well established, this work presents a unique and well-executed combination of both elements. So, I would recommend this paper for publication in Nature Communications, provided the authors more clearly explain the novelty and potential impact of their demonstration, more precisely for the temporal bound mode, and address the minor comments outlined below.
1. Authors mention in the introduction the difference between a PTC bandgap and parametric amplification is the bandgap and the relaxation of phase matching. This explanation is commonly used in literature but requires further elaboration. The reason that there seems to be no phase matching requirement in PTCs is because in theory it is assumed that the whole medium is modulated simultaneously (therefore with k=0) however that is never the case if one uses a propagating pump for modulation. The phase still needs to be matched. Response to Reviewer #1
Dear Reviewer #1:
We sincerely appreciate your supportive comments and thoughtful feedback. Your insights have
given us the opportunity to further clarify and emphasize the key mechanisms behind our research.
Reviewer #1 – General Comments:
“In the manuscript entitled “Observation of wave amplification and temporal topological state in
a genuine photonic time crystal”, Xiong et al. present an impressive and experimentally rich
demonstration of a genuine photonic time crystal (PTC), realized via a dynamically modulated
transmission line platform. Through temporal periodic modulation, they succeed in observing the
emergence of k-gaps and associated phenomena such as wave amplification. Even more
compelling is their direct observation of a temporally localized topological edge state at a domain
wall between two distinct PTC phases. The work is well-structured and highly original. I am
enthusiastic about its potential impact and would recommend publication.”
Response from authors:
Thank you so much for your appreciation and highly positive comment that “Xiong et al. present
an impressive and experimentally rich demonstration of a genuine photonic time crystal (PTC)”,
“The work is well-structured and highly original” and “I am enthusiastic about its potential
impact and would recommend publication”.
In the following, we will fully address your questions point by point.
Reviewer #1 – Comments 1:
“Temporally localized topological edge states have previously been demonstrated in a synthetic
space (e.g., Ref. 20). The authors should explicitly discuss this earlier work and highlight how
their approach differs. That said, to the best of my knowledge, this work indeed represents the first
realization of temporally localized topological edge states in a genuine photonic time crystal, as
opposed to previous implementations based on synthetic dimensions.”
Response from authors:
Thank you very much for your appreciation of our work’s novelty that “this work represents the
first realization of temporally localized topological edge state in a genuine photonic time crystal”.
For further clarification, we provide a systematic comparison of the model and methodology in
the context of recent progress on topological photonic time crystals, showing that our work differs
from the previous studies not only in the methodology but also in the fundamental model.
To the best of our knowledge, only two experimental realizations have been reported in photonic
systems [Feis et al., Nature Photonics (2025): 1-8; Ren et al., Nature Communications 16.1 (2025):
707], along with one preprint in acoustic wave systems [arXiv:2507.04068], and another in elastic
wave systems [arXiv:2306.09627]. In both photonic demonstrations of temporal topological edge
states, as you are aware, time functions as a discrete synthetic dimension—represented by the cycle
number of the pulses circulating in the coupled fiber loops—while the space is mapped to the
relative temporal positions of the pulses within each cycle. Therefore, the observed topological
edge mode emerges in an effectively synthetic “space-time” domain. By contrast, in our system,
enabled by differential modulation, we directly observe the temporal topological edge state in the
actual space-time coordinates.
Moreover, in all the previous works mentioned above, the “momentum bandgap” originates from
the spatial periodical stacking of gain and loss—namely, a non-Hermitian PT-symmetry-broken
Bloch phase. By contrast, the original theoretical prediction attributes the momentum bandgap
solely to temporal periodic modulation of the real part of the refractive index in a spatially
homogeneous Hermitian medium. Our system aligns exactly with this model (Hermitian, spatially
homogenous, real-index modulation), thereby constituting the first realization of a genuine
photonic time crystal.
To further highlight our novelty compared with prior works, we have added an explicit discussion
in the revised manuscript (lines 88-95), directly contrasting our results with the existing study.
“Although temporal localization phenomena have recently been observed in several PT-symmetric
platforms in synthetic space-time [24,25]—where time corresponds to the cycle number of pulses
circulating in the coupled fiber loops and space is represented by the relative temporal positions
of the pulses within each cycle—as well as in non-photonic systems [26,27], the direct observation
of a temporal topological edge state in a genuine PTC within actual space-time has, until now,
remained elusive.”
Reviewer #1 – Comments 2:
“Line 155, the authors mention that “k gaps open in momentum space”. However, in the measured
spectrum in Fig 3b, there is no clear “gap” at k = 0.5, but a dark spot occupying the expected k-
gap region. Could the authors elaborate on this? Is it an experimental artifact, or does it point to
a more nuanced understanding of how k-gaps manifest in this system?”
Response from authors:
Thank you for raising the concern regarding the existence of modes inside a k gap. We would like
to clarify that this originates from the fundamental distinction between conventional photonic
bandgaps (ω-gaps) and k gaps in photonic time crystals (PTCs).
In spatial photonic crystals, ω-gaps prohibit wave propagation due to their evanescent decay: when
excited at a frequency within the ω-gap, waves are totally reflected at a spatial interface and cannot
penetrate the crystal. By contrast, in PTCs, k-gap eigenmodes possess both non-zero real and
imaginary parts of the eigenfrequency. The real part enforces zero group velocity, while the
imaginary part breaks energy conservation and drives temporal amplification. As a result, if a PTC
is excited at a k-gap mode through a temporal interface (as in our experiment), the wave remains
confined within the transmission line and forms stationary amplification, making it directly
observable inside the PTC. This mechanism has been detailed in prior studies on PTCs [19, 22]. It
also explains why the experimentally extracted band structure in Fig. 3b exhibits dark spots
(amplified fields) precisely at the theoretically predicted k-gap regions.
To avoid ambiguity, we have added the following explanation in the revised manuscript (lines
192-195):
“Note that we excite the PTC through a temporal interface. As a result, the k-gap mode, having
zero group velocity, remains confined within the transmission line and undergoes self-
amplification, producing dark spots in the measured dispersion within the gap region.”

Reviewer #2 – Comments 1:
“The authors state that when the incident wave, this being a broad pulse, hits the transmission
line there is power gain around the k-gap coming from the modulation mechanism. They also
mention that k-gap in time crystals is analogous to omega-gap in photonic crystals. When incident

Here when light hits the transmission line it couples in and its intensity enhances in the k-gap

Response from authors:
Thank you for raising the concern about the difference in wave dynamics between an ω-gap and a
k gap. We would like to clarify that although a k gap is formally the mathematical analogue of an
ω-gap, their modal dynamics are fundamentally different.
Mathematically, the term “bandgap” describes an eigenvalue system in which the real part of the
eigenvalue (𝑘 for an ω-gap and Ω for a k gap, with subscripts B and F denoting Bloch and
𝐵 𝐹
Floquet modes, respectively) becomes degenerate, while the imaginary part splits into two
opposite nonzero values. These paired imaginary components give rise to two conjugate
eigenmodes that either grow or decay spatially (in spatial photonic crystals, or SPCs) or temporally
(in photonic time crystals, or PTCs).
Physically, as discussed in [Lyubarov et al. Science 377.6604 (2022): 425-428], the wave
dynamics differ dramatically between a SPC and a PTC at their respective bandgaps. As illustrated
in Fig R4a, when an SPC is excited at a frequency within the ω-gap, energy conservation dictates
that all fields decay rather than grow away from the excitation point. This evanescent spatial
behavior results in total reflection at a spatial interface.
By contrast, as shown in Fig. R4b, when a PTC is excited at a momentum within the k gap, the
breaking of time-translation symmetry violates energy conservation. The system simultaneously
supports both temporally growing and decaying modes, which overall produce a net increase in
energy. Importantly, temporally backscattered waves are forbidden by causality (see dashed line
in Fig. R4b). As a result, when a PTC is excited at its k-gap momentum through a temporal
interface, instead of being spatially reflected, the wave remains “frozen” (due to zero group
velocity) and amplifies within the medium. A similar discussion can be found in [Lustig et al.,
Optica 5.11 (2018): 1390-1395], from which we excerpt their simulated pulse dynamic of both
bulk and k-gap modes in Fig. R4c-d.
Fig. R4. a,b: Eigenmodes in an SPC (a) and PTC (b). Excerpted from [Lyubarov et al. Science
377.6604 (2022): 425-428]. c,d: FDTD simulated wave dynamics in PTC, when the wave
momentum components reside in the band and in the k gap. Excerpted from [Lustig et al.,
Optica 5.11 (2018): 1390-1395].
Accordingly, we have added the following clarifications in the Introduction and Section III to
distinguish between ω gaps and k gaps, and to explain the wave dynamics associated with
incidence into a PTC.
(lines 64-70) “In contrast to the spatially evanescent modes of conventional photonic bandgaps, k

accounts for the stationarity, while the nonzero imaginary part of the eigenfrequency drives
amplification. When a k gap is excited through a temporal interface, rather than being spatially
reflected, the pulse remains inside the medium with a growing temporal amplitude [18].”
(lines 203-208) “When a pulse with a broad momentum spectrum is incident on a PTC, it
encounters a purely temporal boundary—unlike the spatial boundary of a conventional photonic
crystal, which enforces total reflection. Under momentum conservation, all momentum
components of the incident wave lying on the original light line map onto the PTC band structure.”

1. Where does the temporal boundary come from?
We apologize for not sufficiently illustrating the physical meaning of the term “temporal
interface” in the section on the temporal topological edge state. In Fig. R5a we plot the
temporal profiles of two PTCs with distinct Zak phases. As predicted in [Lustig et al.,
Optica 5.11 (2018): 1390-1395], the quantized Zak phase is protected by temporal mirror
symmetry, with the two symmetry centers corresponding to Zak phases of 0 and 𝜋. When
two PTCs with different Zak phases are aligned in time, a domain-wall structure forms,
and a temporal topological edge state emerges. When the two PTCs contact each other, as
shown in Fig. R5b, a temporal discontinuity appears at t = 0, which constitutes the physical
meaning of the “temporal interface”.
Fig. R5: Temporal permittivity profiles for pure PTCs and the domain-wall structure. a. The
temporal profiles of PTCs with different Zak phases, 𝜃 = 0 (blue) and 𝜃 = 𝜋 (red).
𝑍𝑎𝑘 𝑍𝑎𝑘

t=0, a temporal interface abruptly changes the permittivity.
2. How do the two DTL terminal ports (spatial boundaries) affect the experimental result and
what design considerations are involved?
Your concern regarding the spatial boundaries is indeed critical. Although we carefully
considered this issue in our design, we regret not including these details in our original
manuscript.
The two spatial ports affect the experiment in several ways. Firstly, the impedance
matching between the DTL and transition sections at both ends needs to be carefully
considered. To be concise, a trade-off is required between complete matching (ideal for
initial pulse injection) and complete mismatch (theoretically forming an ideal resonator
with no energy leakage, facilitating energy accumulation in the amplification process).
Secondly, when exciting the k gaps (Fig. 3e), a broadband pulse is injected that contains
both bulk-band and k-gap momenta. Since bulk-band modes propagate while k-gap modes
are stationary, the two components gradually separate. Escape of bulk-band modes through
the ports, though much weaker than the amplified k-gap modes, makes the practical DTL
deviate from an ideal infinitely long PTC.
Lastly, the two spatial boundaries naturally form a windowed system, which restricts the
momentum-space resolution and induces spectral broadening. This effect will be discussed
explicitly in our response to your Comment 8.
To address these factors, in our experiment we used an optimized impedance configuration:
28.33Ω for the DTL Bloch impedance and 50Ω for the characteristic impedance of the
transition sections. This choice strikes a balance between efficient signal injection and clear
observation of amplification. Furthermore, we carefully tuned the circuit and modulation
parameters so that the key physical phenomena—the k-gap topology in the transmission
spectrum (Fig. 4b in the main text) and the temporal edge state (Fig. 4d in the main text)
—are clearly observed within a short time window after modulation onset, thereby
minimizing adverse effects from bulk-mode escape and spectral broadening.
Accordingly, we have added Fig. R5 as Fig. 4a and 4b in the revised manuscript to clarify the
temporal boundary, and included a new section in the Supplementary Materials to elaborate on
spatial boundary effects as Section IX: Spatial boundary influence and design considerations.

enhancements, the phenomenon observed in this work, i.e. temporal exponential energy growth,
stemming from the non-zero imaginary part of eigenfrequency in k-gap modes. Below we will

Let us start with the first paper [B. Corcoran et al, Nature Photonics volume 3, pages 206–210
(2009)]. As described in the caption of Fig.1 from the first paper that: “The fundamental pulse at

Similarly, the second paper [Foteinopoulou and Vigneron, Phys. Rev. B 88, 195144 (2013)]
discusses the field enhancement in a plasmonic slow light biwaveguide by another mechanism. As
discussed in Section VI that “EM energy, E, is fed into the biwaveguide from above via the ATR
prism, at a faster rate than its relaxation sideways in the +x direction (M2 is a forward mode),
because of the ultralow energy velocity of the M2 mode.”, the energy velocity (group velocity)
mismatch results in energy accumulation in the slow-light system(as shown in Fig. R7b) and
therefore enhances the EM wave intensity. When the system reaches a steady state, the total energy
is also time-invariant (Fig. R7c).
Fig R7: a. the schematic of slow light enhanced non-linearity, where the inset points out that total
photon number is conserved. Adopted from [B. Corcoran et al, Nature Photonics volume 3, pages
206–210 (2009)]. b. the schematic of slow light assisted energy accumulation, highlighting a

In general, in a passive photonic system without loss, the total photon number is always conserved.
However, in the k-gap mode of a PTC, although the real part of group velocity 𝑑𝜔/𝑑𝑡 is zero,
instead of being compressed or accumulated, the incident pulse undergoes stationary amplification
with its spatial line shape extended. Such amplification is the consequence of the non-zero
imaginary part of eigenfrequency Ω, and pulse dynamic simulations have been demonstrated in
many literatures [Lustig et al., Optica 5.11 (2018): 1390-1395, Sharabi et al., Optica 9.6 (2022):
585-592.]. This denotes the distinction between a k gap and a conventional photonic slow-light
system.

(lines 66-76), where some comments are added to compare the amplification mechanisms:
“…Here, the vanishing group velocity accounts for the stationarity, while the nonzero imaginary
part of the eigenfrequency drives amplification. When a k gap is excited through a temporal
interface, rather than being spatially reflected, the pulse remains inside the medium with a growing
temporal amplitude [18]. Such amplification breaks energy conservation law, thereby greatly differ
from passive slow-light system supporting energy accumulation and field enhancement [19,20].
Moreover, since the spatially uniform modulation and conjugated eigenmodes in k gap naturally
satisfy phase matching condition [21], temporal modulation induces non-resonant amplification
over the entire k gap, but is maximized at the mid-gap, providing a mechanism of coherent light
generation [22] (e.g., lasers) by drawing energy from time modulation rather than gain media”

“The authors use a model to calculate the permittivity versus the DC bias for different values of

Response from authors:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable comment regarding the finite response time of varactors.
Below we present the varactor latency mechanisms and demonstrate their negligible impact in our
experimental system, which employs the GaAs-based Skyworks SMV1249-079LF varactor.
1. Carrier transit-time limitation
The depletion width adjustment under time-varying modulation is delayed by the finite carrier
transit time. With a typical carrier mobility of 8500cm2/(V⋅s), depletion region width of ~0.1-1μm,
and built-in potential on the order of volts, the transit time is typically tens of ps. This is negligible
compared to our 7.7ns modulation period.
2. Series resistance effect
The total series resistance (including bulk, contact, and packaging resistances) and junction
capacitance form a low-pass filter, and introduce an extra RC delay. Considering that the
SMV1249 varactor has a series resistance of 0.6Ω (according to the Skyworks SMV1249
Datasheet) and junction capacitance of 25pF (at operating point), their multiplication renders an
RC delay of ~15ps, which is also insignificant at low frequencies (e.g. 130 MHz in our modulation).
3. Trap-assisted response delay
Deep-level traps (e.g., the EL2 in GaAs) could introduce longer time constants. However, the
Skyworks SMV1249 employs high-purity MBE-grown GaAs and renders trap-related hysteresis
negligible at 130 MHz.
The above interpretation is supported by prior studies on PTCs with similar varactors ([27], [28]
in the main text) and is further validated by the excellent agreement between our theoretical and
experimental results. As you suggested, we have added the following clarification in the revised
manuscript (lines 129-139):
“Note in our experiment, we employ the Skyworks SMV1249-079LF varactor. Based on critical
parameters from the datasheet (including series resistance), typical junction characteristics (carrier
mobility, depletion region width, and built-in potential), and our modulation parameters, the finite
time delay caused by carrier transit-time and series resistance effect can be estimated to be on the
order of picoseconds, which is negligible compared to our 7.7ns modulation period. Meanwhile,
the high-purity MBE-grown Skyworks SMV1249 also exhibits negligible trap-related hysteresis
at low frequencies. These considerations regarding varactor latency are supported by prior studies
[28, 32], and are further validated by the agreement between theoretical and experimental results
presented in subsequent sections.”

Regarding your comment that “provided the authors more clearly explain the novelty and potential

first offer a general response to both concerns.
Concerns 1: “the novelty for the demonstration of temporal bound mode”
Topological photonics incorporating time has attracted increasing attention in recent years. As the
most representative phenomenon, the temporal topological edge state has never been observed in
a classical wave system. The main challenge lies in the direct observation of a “k gap” which
requires both perfect separation of modulation and excitation signal and a relatively large
modulation region. Therefore, all the experimental demonstrations of topological PTC are
conducted in synthetic space-time lattices and “pseudo momentum gap” arising from PT symmetry
broken phase [Feis et al., Nature Photonics (2025): 1-8, and Ren et al., Nature Communications
16.1 (2025): 707], which is not a genuine PTC. In this work, we have observed the real space-time
evolution of the mode dynamics in a k gap, extracted the quantized Zak phases with physical
observables (phase differences between transmission and reflection), and more importantly,
demonstrated the direct detection of a temporal topological edge that can focus light in time.
Concerns 2: “potential impact of their demonstration of temporal bound mode”
From an experimental perspective, by combining the existing experiment methods with our
innovation in the differential modulation, we establish a protocol of “in situ” observation of a
temporal modulated system. Such an approach has the potential to be generalized to space-time
modulated systems and even higher order space-time varying systems.
From a physical perspective, the ability to focus light in time, or in other words, generating ultra-
fast lasers pulses, holds major implications for electron spectroscopy and strong-field physics and
won the Nobel prize in 2023. The existing methods for generating ultra-fast lasers primarily rely
on enhancing the material non-linearity and exploiting higher harmonic generation. Temporal
topological edge mode, by contrast, provides another fundamentally different and robust pathway
toward realizing ultrafast lasers.

Response from authors:
Thank you for pointing out the core mechanism of differential modulation, which represents a
major technical advancement of our experiment protocol. Below we’ll explicitly explain the
necessity of differential modulation, which renders the out-of-phase modulation for each varactor
pair, but achieves the actual in-phase modulation across all varactor pairs along the line.
As you certainly know, all the previous efforts in realization of PTCs in the microwave regime,
employed experimental protocols with a single varactor in each unit cell (transmission line,
metasurface, waveguide, etc.). Such a configuration inevitably couples the modulation signal into
the core circuit. Moreover, to maintain the modulation strength of the varactor, the modulation
voltages are normally set much higher than the seed signal itself. Consequently, the transmitting
signal becomes obscured by the much stronger modulation signal, making it difficult to isolate and
exclusively observe its space-time evolution in a PTC.
To overcome this limitation, we implemented the differential modulation scheme (Fig. 2c and Fig.
S1a) using a pair of opposite polarized varactors in each unit cell. As shown in Fig. S1b in
Supplementary Materials, this design achieves the desired dual functionality:
1. The large but out-of-phase modulation voltages of each varactor pair cancel out along the trace
line, creating a relatively “quiet” environment for transmitting signal direct detection.
2. Each varactors pair maintains an identical time-varying phase (note the opposite polarity loading
relative to the microstrip trace line), thus meeting the in-phase modulation requirement for PTC
implementation by DTL. Therefore, in general, our DTL-realized equivalent PTC is still under
purely temporal modulation.
As highlighted in our manuscript’s introduction and conclusion, this design represents a significant
advancement over prior time-varying platforms.
Accordingly, to emphasize the necessity of the differential modulation scheme, and its role in
achieving pure temporal modulation for constructing an equivalent PTC, we re-organized the
Section II of Supplementary Materials and added the following texts/modifications to the revised
manuscript (lines 140-145)
“In conventional DTL designs, the transmitting signal along the DTL and the external varactor
modulation remain inherently coupled, preventing clear observation of wave temporal dynamics
in the realized PTC. To overcome this limitation, we adopt a differential modulation scheme in
which each pair of varactors is reverse-biased with opposite polarities and symmetrically placed
on either side of the microstrip trace line in each unit cell.”

After Lustig et al proposed the concept of PTC and discusses the topological properties [Lustig et
al., Optica 5.11 (2018): 1390-1395], several experiments have been reported in publication or
preprints. The first realization of a PTC, as you mentioned in Comment 5, is based on a dynamic

More recently, experiments have progressed toward realizing a temporal topological edge state:
two in photonic system [Feis et al. Nature Photonics (2025): 1-8, and Ren et al. Nature
Communications 16.1 (2025): 707], one preprint work in acoustic wave system [arXiv:2507.04068]
and one preprint work in elastic wave system [arXiv:2306.09627]. In the two photonic realizations
of temporal topological edge states, time serves as a synthetic space, i.e. the cycle number of the

positions for the pulses in each cycle. Therefore, the observed topological edge mode resides in a
space-time dual-synthetic space. Moreover, due to the lack of phase measurement methods of each
pulse, the observation of k-space properties of PTC are unreachable. In our system, with the

topological edge state in the real space-time dynamics.

merely emerges from the temporal periodic modulation of the real part of the refractive index from
a spatial homogeneous Hermitian media. Our model perfectly maps to the theoretical model
(Hermitian, spatial homogenous, modulation on the real part), thereby our realization is the first
genuine 1D photonic time crystal with sufficient crystal periods.

### Reviewer 1

In the manuscript entitled “Observation of wave amplification and temporal topological state in a genuine photonic time crystal”, Xiong et al. present an impressive and experimentally rich demonstration of a genuine photonic time crystal (PTC), realized via a dynamically modulated transmission line platform. Through temporal periodic modulation, they succeed in observing the emergence of k-gaps and associated phenomena such as wave amplification. Even more compelling is their direct observation of a temporally localized topological edge state at a domain wall between two distinct PTC phases. The work is well-structured and highly original. I am enthusiastic about its potential impact and would recommend publication, pending the authors' response to the following points:
- Temporally localized topological edge states have previously been demonstrated in a synthetic space (e.g., Ref. 20). The authors should explicitly discuss this earlier work and highlight how their approach differs. That said, to the best of my knowledge, this work indeed represents the first realization of temporally localized topological edge states in a genuine photonic time crystal, as opposed to previous implementations based on synthetic dimensions.
- Line 155, the authors mention that “k gaps open in momentum space”. However, in the measured spectrum in Fig 3b, there is no clear “gap” at k = 0.5, but a dark spot occupying the expected k-gap region. Could the authors elaborate on this? Is it an experimental artifact, or does it point to a more nuanced understanding of how k-gaps manifest in this system?
- Line 195, as the authors mentioned, the system exhibits intrinsic loss. Given that the Floquet band structure is calculated under lossless conditions, how robust is the comparison between theory and experiment? Could the inclusion of loss qualitatively or quantitatively alter the Floquet features?
- The observation of a temporal topological edge state is one of the most exciting aspects of this work. To better understand and reproduce this result, the authors should provide the precise temporal modulation profiles corresponding to the two PTCs with Zak phases of 0 and π, respectively. Also, please include the exact modulation used to form the temporal domain wall.
- In Fig. 1f, the temporal edge state is expected to exhibit nearly unity transmission. Yet in Fig. 4b, the measured |T + R| is close to zero. This striking difference deserves clarification—could it arise from interference effects, mode mismatch, or other loss mechanisms?
- The asymmetry in the temporal edge state profile is intriguing. The authors suggest it stems from intrinsic losses in the transmission line (lines 258–260). Can this be backed up with simulations or theoretical modeling? If so, showing such analysis would greatly strengthen the manuscript.

### Reviewer 2

This is a very timely and interesting study of a time crystalline system experimentally realized in the microwave regime via a transmission line comprising an inductor and a varactor diode element, the latter having bias-controlled capacitance. With a time-modulated bias it hence corresponds to a time-modulated permittivity system.
The authors show a power gain in the system occurring within the k-gap of the time-modulated system, as well as new type of topological edge modes in the phase-space of the time-crystalline system which were observed when an interface is created between the two time crystals, each having a different modulation phase.
This work reports exciting new Physics that I believe will inspire further progress in the field of space-time photonics. I am therefore recommending its publication provided the authors explain more in depth the underlying Physics, while giving more expanded supportive context for the benefit of the reader.
In particular:
(1) The authors state that when the incident wave, this being a broad pulse, hits the transmission line there is power gain around the k-gap coming from the modulation mechanism. They also mention that k-gap in time crystals is analogous to omega-gap in photonic crystals. When incident light within the omega-gap spectrum hits the photonic crystal interface it completely back-reflects. Here when light hits the transmission line it couples in and its intensity enhances in the k-gap spectrum. So, it appears the analogy does not quite work- something is different in their system because the EM can couples into the k-gap modes. Can the authors say a few words what allows the wave to couple into the k-gap modes, instead of getting back-reflected as one would expect from a k-gap behavior.
(2) I think it would be helpful if the authors added a section in the supplemental material explaining the boundary conditions they are considering. In section IV they are talking about temporal boundaries but the modulation is continuous with no discontinuity so I am a bit confused where the temporal boundary (i.e. a discontinuity in permittivity in time) comes from. Also, while the wave goes through the transmission line there are clearly spatial boundaries. Elaborating further these aspects would be very helpful not only in understanding the method but also the results.

In spatial photonic crystals the frequency is fixed by the input wave and the Floquet-Bloch wave inside the photonic crystal is a sum of various spatial harmonics, i.e., wave vector components, that relate to the spatial modulation (i.e. spatial period a). Here, the Floquet wave inside the time crystal should be a sum of different time harmonics that relate to the modulation frequency, right? ### Reviewer 3

In the paper, authors experimentally demonstrate both nonhermitian bandgap and temporal topological state at the temporal boundary of two bandgaps with different topologies. Although the former has been demonstrated the latter is a first-time demonstration to my knowledge. They employ a transmission line based method to mimic photonic time crystal in microwave regime. The paper is well structured and written with sufficient technical details provided in the main text and supplementary. Although similar experimental setups have been used in previous proof-of-concept demonstrations of temporally varying media, and the theoretical foundations of topology in photonic time crystals are well established, this work presents a unique and well-executed combination of both elements. The phase still needs to be matched. And, as mentioned in the supplementary it is still important to control the phase between the varactors of adjacent unit cells in the experimental realization to observe the amplification. That is still part of the phase matching requirement. So, the amplification in OPA and PTCs are still fundamentally linked to each other.
